I2534.bio: Electa Wiltse was born 17 January 1818 in Sterling, Cayuga County, New York, a daughter of John Sterling Wiltse and Joanna Barnes, and one of at least eleven siblings who settled in the Maumee valley. On 11 March 1835 (Find a Grave gives 1834/1835) she married Peter Burdo (Bordeaux, 1806-1869), a French-descended pioneer whose family had lived at the mouth of the Maumee since 1806 and at Maumee City since 1813, as Peter himself told the Pioneers Association in 1866. They had eleven children, including Noah, Lavisa, Lois, Eliza, Clarisa, Albert, Winfield Scott, Ellen and Belle. Electa died 16 November 1886, aged 68, and is buried beside Peter in Section 17-A of Springfield Township Cemetery, Holland, Lucas County; her stone reads 'Electa Burdo, Age 69 Years'.

I2523.bio: Peter Burdo (Bordeaux) was born 7 May 1806 near the River Raisin at Monroe, Michigan, to French-Canadian settlers Louis Bourdeaux (1771-1821) and Marie-Suzanne Gaillard; his father moved from Fort Wayne to Detroit, to the mouth of the Maumee in 1806 and to Maumee in 1813, and Peter settled at Maumee in 1815, making him one of its earliest residents. He married Electa Wiltse (1818-1886) in March 1835 and they raised eleven children, including Noah (a Civil War soldier), Lavisa (grandmother of the Toledo Schmitts), Lois, Eliza, Clarisa, Albert, Winfield Scott, Ellen and Belle. An 1866 Pioneers Association address by Willard V. Way, printed in the Toledo Daily Blade on 5 July 1866, quoted him on the French families already living on the Maumee when he arrived. He died 7 January 1869 at Maumee and is buried with Electa in Springfield Township Cemetery, Holland, Ohio (Section 17-A).

I112.bio: The immigrant ancestor of the Wiltsee/Wiltse family. Contemporary records call him 'born in Copenhagen'; he first appears at Fort Orange (Albany) in 1658 as a soldier and French-speaking escort for a Mohawk party to Trois-Rivières. He recorded marriage intentions with Margrietje Meyers in New Amsterdam on 10 Jan 1660, served in the Esopus (Wiltwyck/Kingston) garrison, was captured with a child in the 7 June 1663 Indian attack on Wiltwyck and later freed, was a corporal of the burgher guard in 1665, and from c.1669 farmed near Hellgate in Newtown, Long Island, buying a 77-acre farm in 1681 and becoming a patentee of Dongan's Newtown Patent (1686). He remarried in 1705 and last appears in 1707; the traditional death date of 1712 is unverified. The link to Philippe Maton Wiltsee as father comes from the discredited 1908 Jerome Wiltsee memoir and is rejected by Zabriskie (NYGBR 1975-77).

I116.bio: Traditional (Jerome Wiltsee 1895/1908 memoir) founder of the family: a Walloon dyer from Tourcoing/'Fourcoin' said to have married Sophia Ter Bosch at Leiden in 1616, sailed on the New Netherland in 1623 (or 1632), and been killed by Indians at the Swaanendael (Zwaanendael) colony on the Delaware in March 1632. Leiden records do show a Philippe Maton, widower from Tourcoing, marrying Philippote Caron at the Walloon Church in 1599 and admitted as a free citizen ('lintreder') in 1619, but researchers (Zabriskie, NYGBR 1975-77; Trudy Bray) found no evidence that he was the father of Hendrick Martensen, whose patronymic implies a father named Marten. Treat the Maton-Wiltsee connection as unproven.

I144.bio: Immigrant ancestor of the Van Wyck family, born c.1641 at Wijk bij Duurstede, Utrecht, Netherlands, son of Berndt Danielse van Wyck and Anneken Cornelisse van den Engh. He came to New Netherland about 1660, settled at Midwout (Flatbush) with 100 acres and bought another 100 acres in 1664 for 240 pounds. He married Anna Polhemius, daughter of Flatbush's first minister, about 1666-67; both were Flatbush church members in 1667. He took the oath of allegiance to William of Orange in 1687, made a joint will with Anna on 17 June 1684, and died at Flatbush 23 June 1713.

I146.bio: Born c.1598 at Boikirchen, perhaps Zweikirchen near Wolfstein in the Palatinate (Germany); matriculated at Heidelberg University 26 Jan 1620 as 'Johannes Theodorus Polhemius dictus Hammerstein'. He served Reformed congregations in the Palatinate and at Gieten (1624-27) and Meppel in Drenthe, then sailed in 1635-36 to Dutch Brazil, where he ministered at Pernambuco, Itamaracá (c.1638-42), Goiana, Rio Grande and Paraíba, was scribe of the Brazil classis in 1638 and owned a plantation on Itamaracá. After the Portuguese reconquest he sailed on the St. Charles to New Amsterdam in 1654 and in October 1654 became the first Dutch Reformed minister of Midwout (Flatbush), also serving Brooklyn and Amersfoort 1656-60. He died at Flatbush c.8 June 1676 and was buried in the Flatbush church on 11 June 1676.

I207.bio: A Yorkshireman (christened 19 Apr 1603 at Halifax per one compiled source; other sources give 1586), Cambridge B.A. 1622-23, deacon at Peterborough 1622-23, and for about seven years curate of Coley Chapel near Halifax. A Puritan with strong Presbyterian views, he emigrated to New England (compiled sources: 1635 on the James), ministered at Wethersfield and Stamford, Connecticut, and in 1644 led families to Hempstead, Long Island, where he founded what is today Christ's First Presbyterian Church, often called the first Presbyterian church in America. Cotton Mather praised him; Dutch ministers Megapolensis and Drisius reported in 1657 and 1659 on his wish to return to England because of irregular salary and his wife's ill health. He returned c.1659 and died in England in 1662/63 (compiled sources say Essex; one article says a Yorkshire tombstone). Sons Daniel (author of A Brief Description of New-York, 1670) and Nathaniel helped found Jamaica, L.I.

I2408.bio: Immigrant ancestor, born 9 Apr 1638 at Saint-Jean-de-Sauves (Vienne, Poitou), near Loudun, France, and baptized at nearby La Chaussée, son of Mathurin Binet and Marie Proulx. On 23 Mar 1665 at Loudun he signed a three-year indenture (60 livres a year) with La Rochelle merchant Pierre Gaigner and sailed from La Rochelle on Le Cat on 27 Apr 1665 with 66 other engagés, reaching Quebec 18 June 1665. Placed as a servant with Henri Pinguet (1666 census), he received 40 arpents from the Jesuits at Petite-Auvergne (Charlesbourg) on 16 Mar 1666 and married Catherine Bourgeois, a Fille du Roi from Rouen, at Notre-Dame de Québec on 19 Oct 1667. The family moved to Beauport by 1673, where he died 15 May 1699. Avenue Binet in Charlesbourg bears the name.

I122.bio: 1885 county-history sketch (paraphrased): William Prosser was born in Erie County, Pennsylvania, 12 Sep 1802, and married Mary Lefler there in 1829; she was born 26 Sep 1808 (the book says 'Canton County', probably Centre County, PA, which Find a Grave gives). They spent their early married life in Ohio (Ashland County, where the children were born) and in 1853 came to DeKalb County, Indiana, settling on section 10 of Jackson Township, where he was 'one of the most prominent citizens of the county' until his death on 9 May 1881. Twelve children were born to them, nine of whom came to DeKalb County with their parents: Nancy (Mrs. John Lawhead), Henry, Adam, William S., Joseph C., Sarah (Mrs. Daniel Stroh), Elizabeth (Mrs. John A. Provines), Maria (Mrs. Jacob B. Coy) and Mary (Mrs. Samuel Goodwin); James came in 1854 and lived in Auburn; the eldest, John, died Oct 1851 in his 22nd year and the youngest died in infancy, Mar 1853. In 1885 the widow was still living on the old homestead with son Joseph C. Separate sketches in the same book cover sons Adam (Co. C, 88th Indiana; wounded at Atlanta) and Joseph C. (Co. A, 100th Indiana; 18 battles, marched with Sherman to the sea). He is buried in Evergreen Cemetery, Auburn, with the inscription 'Aged 78y 7m 27d'; Find a Grave names his father as Daniel Prosser (1744-1829).

I1217.bio: 1885 county-history sketch (paraphrased): Samuel Goodwin, 'one of the old settlers and representative citizens of Union Township,' was born in Centre County, Pennsylvania in October 1816 (Find a Grave and the 1920 history give 1817), the second of seven children of David and Catherine (Zimmerman) Goodwin. In 1822 the family moved to Wayne County, Ohio, and then to Ashland County, where the father died and Samuel grew up. He married Elizabeth Good in 1843 and in 1854 moved to DeKalb County, Indiana, settling on a heavily timbered tract a mile west of Waterloo which he cleared into a 115-acre farm with large, comfortable buildings. Elizabeth died in 1865 leaving Mary E. (Keck), Leander S., Joseph W., Lucy (George) and Alice (Atwood); he then married Mrs. Mary J. (Prosser) Brubaker and had Ina, Frank and William F. The 1920 history adds that his brothers David and Daniel also came to DeKalb County and that 'as they had adjoining land the three families constituted almost a community'; he was a Whig, then Republican, first Evangelical and later United Brethren. He died 15 Feb 1889 and is buried in Waterloo Cemetery. His father David Goodwin (1782-1849, a War of 1812 veteran) is buried at Redhaw, Ashland County, Ohio.

I553.bio: 1914 county-history sketches (paraphrased, from the biographies of his son William D. Goodwin, pp. 793-795, and son-in-law Simon Dilgard): Daniel Goodwin was born in Wayne County, Ohio, 2 Oct 1824, son of David and Catherine (Zimmerman) Goodwin, and grew up in Ashland County. On 28 Jun 1850 in Ashland County he married Mary Ann (the book says 'Mary S.') Barron, born in Wayne County 2 Aug 1830, who bore Philemon (14/15 May 1851, Ohio) and Henry (Sep 1854, Indiana) and died 24 Sep 1854. He first came to DeKalb County in 1853, entered/bought 208 acres in Smithfield Township, returned to Ohio and brought his family in May 1854. On 26 Apr 1855 he married Susannah Kiefer and had William (1856), Eliza (1858, m. Simon Dilgard), Elmira (1860, m. Curtis Parnell), John W. (1862) and David (1866). Except for five years living in Waterloo, he farmed the Smithfield Township homestead (section 33) until his death there on 2 Jul 1903 (Find a Grave stone reads 4 Jul). He is buried in Waterloo Cemetery; the 1920 history notes that he, Samuel and David Goodwin held adjoining land near Waterloo and 'constituted almost a community.'

I664.bio: Mary Ann Barron (the 1914 history prints 'Mary S. Barron') was born in Wayne County, Ohio, 2 Aug 1830, and married Daniel Goodwin in Ashland County, Ohio on 28 Jun 1850. She bore two sons, Philemon (May 1851, Ohio) and Henry A. (Sep 1854, Indiana), moving with Daniel to Smithfield Township, DeKalb County, Indiana in May 1854. She died 24 Sep 1854, shortly after Henry's birth; the 1914 history says she lived 'but a short time after their marriage.' No Find a Grave memorial was located for her; Philemon's memorial and the Waterloo Cemetery inscription book name her as his mother, and her 1854 grave is probably unmarked or in a Smithfield Township pioneer plot. I995.bio: Susannah Kiefer was born 21 Sep 1828 in Berks County, Pennsylvania (one 1914 sketch says Delaware County), daughter of Jacob Kiefer (1798-1888) and Catherine Smith (1800-1853). She moved with her parents to Ohio at about age eight and lived in Wayne County about ten miles from Wooster. On 26 Apr 1855 she married the widower Daniel Goodwin and came at once to Smithfield Township, DeKalb County, Indiana, where she raised his two sons and bore William (1856), Eliza (Dilgard), Elmira (Parnell), John W. and David. In 1914, aged about 85, she was still on the home place making a home for her unmarried stepson Henry, 'where she enjoys the respect of all who know her.' I238.bio: Joseph H. Brinkman was born about 1802-1804 in the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg (Find a Grave gives 1804; the tree's 28 Oct 1802 is within range), emigrated in 1834-35, and on 26 Nov 1835 married Elizabeth Kloevkorn at St. John the Baptist, Glandorf - one of the first marriages in the colony. He appears as head of household in the 1840 census (Ottawa Twp) and 1850 census (Greensburg Twp, farmer, real estate $550), three doors from his brother John H. Brinkman (1802-1890, a butcher who came 1837). 1880 Putnam County history (paraphrased from the sketches of sons Franz and John Andrew Brinkman): Joseph Brinkman came from Germany into Putnam County in 1835 with his wife Elizabeth Klavekorn [Klövekorn] and settled in Greensburg Township, part of Father Horstmann's Glandorf colony founded 1834. Their son Franz (b. Greensburg Twp 16 Jan 1841) was a wagon and carriage maker at Ottawa who married Maria Elizabeth Shoemaker at Glandorf 12 May 1869; son John Andrew (b. 10 May 1846) was a carriage and wagon blacksmith who married Mary Kathrina Beckmann (b. Prussia 26 May 1851) at Glandorf in 1871 - the Beckman link in this tree. A G. B. Brinkman (b. 18 Apr 1844 Greensburg Twp, later Jackson Twp) is sketched separately and may be another son. He died in Greensburg Township on or about 6-12 Oct 1866 (Find a Grave cites the Glandorf church death register, age 62) and was buried in St. John's pioneer cemetery, Glandorf, whose stones were later built into the 'Mother of Grace' shrine.

I219.bio: The 'Jacob van Asch van Wijck / Anna van Rijnevelt' parentage of Cornelis Barentse Van Wyck comes from Anne Van Wyck's 1912 book and Provost's Early Settlers of Bushwick (p.129), which gives Jacob as born c.1620 with son Cornelis b. c.1640. Modern research (WikiTree Van_Wyck-8) rejects it: Cornelis Barentsen van Wyck was born 11 Apr 1641 at Wijk bij Duurstede, Utrecht, son of Berndt (Barent) Danielse van Wyck (b. c.1612 Schalkwijk) and Anneken Cornelisse van den Engh - the patronymic 'Barentse' itself implies a father Barent, not Jacob. Recommend treating this generation as a disproven noble-descent claim.
